citations.quote:
Fix a based closed disk $D$ and a finite even subset $B\subset\partial D$. A smoothing is a compact smooth one-manifold in $D$, with boundary precisely $B$ and fixed radial collars there; it may contain circles. A morphism from $P$ to $Q$ is a compact orientable, not separately oriented, smooth surface with corners in $D\times[0,1]$, with bottom $P$, top $Q$, side boundary $B\times[0,1]$ and fixed product collars. Identify surfaces by ambient isotopy relative to these boundary collars. Take free abelian morphism groups, compose by stacking, and impose the following relations in every surrounding surface: a sphere component is zero; a torus component may be deleted with factor $2$; and $C_{12}+C_{34}=C_{13}+C_{24}$, where $C_{ij}$ attaches a tube between disk patches $i,j$ among four disjoint patches in a ball. Denote the resulting category by $\mathcal C(B)$.

For a surface $C$ set $\deg C=\chi(C)-|B|/2$. Permit formal shifts $P\{a\}$, with a surface of degree $e$ having degree $e+b-a$ as a map $P\{a\}\to Q\{b\}$. Take finite direct sums with matrices of morphisms. A complex is a bounded cochain complex in this additive category, whose differential has internal degree zero. A chain map has cochain degree zero; all homotopies have cochain degree $-1$. Unless specified otherwise, maps and homotopies have internal degree zero. Two chain maps are homotopic when $f-g=dh+hd$. Write $K(B)$ for the category with these complexes as objects and chain maps modulo homotopy as morphisms. Call a complex simple if its invertible endomorphisms in $K(B)$ of internal degree zero are exactly the two maps $\pm\operatorname{id}$ (allowing coincidence when the object is zero).

A planar template is a disk with finitely many numbered input disks removed and a properly embedded one-manifold of arcs and circles in the remainder, meeting each boundary in its prescribed marked points. It acts on smoothings by insertion, and on surfaces by insertion in the template crossed with $[0,1]$. Extend by multilinearity to finite sums. For ordered complexes $C_1,\ldots,C_s$ its totalization has term $\bigoplus_{r_1+\cdots+r_s=r}D(C_1^{r_1},\ldots,C_s^{r_s})$, with shifts added, and differential $\sum_i(-1)^{r_1+\cdots+r_{i-1}}D(1,\ldots,d_i,\ldots,1)$ on that summand. For homogeneous maps $f_i$ of cochain degrees $a_i$, use the sign $(-1)^{\sum_i a_i\sum_{j<i}r_j}$ on $D(f_1,\ldots,f_s)$, evaluated on the input summand of degrees $(r_j)$; this is the usual tensor sign convention, independently of the internal grading.

Assume countable choice. Let $S\subset S^3$ be the image of a smooth embedding of the standard $S^2$. There is a smooth ambient isotopy $H_t:S^3\to S^3$, with $H_0=\operatorname{id}$, such that $H_1(S)$ is the standard equatorial sphere $E$. In particular $S^3\setminus S$ has exactly two components. Their closures $B_+$ and $B_-$ are smoothly embedded standard closed $3$-balls with common boundary $S$. If $D_+$ and $D_-$ denote the standard closed hemispheres bounded by $E$, the labels can be chosen so that the restrictions $H_1:B_\pm\to D_\pm$ are diffeomorphisms with the same boundary restriction $H_1|_S:S\to E$. Thus the ball identifications are compatible on their boundary and on a common two-sided collar of that boundary.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$.

1. **Compact main case.** Let $M$ be a compact smooth manifold, possibly with boundary, let $N$ be a smooth manifold without boundary, let $F:M\times I\to N$ be a smooth isotopy of embeddings that is constant near the ends of $I$, and let $W$ be an open neighbourhood of $F(M\times I)$ in $N$. Then there is an ambient isotopy $H:N\times I\to N$ with $H_0=\mathrm{id}_N$, every $H_t$ a diffeomorphism, $H_t\circ F_0=F_t$ for all $t\in I$, $H_t=\mathrm{id}_N$ outside $W$ for every $t$, and $H_t$ stationary near the ends; if $F$ is constant near the ends with parameter $\varepsilon$, then $H_t=\mathrm{id}_N$ for $t\le\varepsilon/2$ and $H_t=H_1$ for $t\ge1-\varepsilon/2$.
2. **Relative form.** Let $N$ be boundaryless, $U\subseteq N$ open, $A\subseteq U$ compact, and let $F:U\times I\to N$ be a smooth isotopy of embeddings whose track image is open in $N\times I$. Then there is a compactly supported ambient isotopy $H$ of $N$ with $H_t\circ F_0=F_t$ on a neighbourhood of $A$ for every $t$.
3. **Boundary stratum.** If $N$ has boundary and $F(M\times I)\subseteq\partial N$, then the ambient isotopy of clause 1 can be chosen with every $H_t$ carrying $\partial N$ onto itself; if $F(M\times I)\subseteq N\setminus\partial N$, it can be chosen compactly supported in $N\setminus\partial N$.
4. **General isotopies.** For the same compact source (possibly with boundary) and boundaryless target as in clause 1, every smooth isotopy extends with support in a compact subset of any prescribed neighbourhood $W$ of $F(M\times I)$. The endpoint-constancy hypothesis and the stationary-end conclusion are both omitted; all other conclusions of clause 1 hold.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. A compact $C^2$ surface, with regular $C^2$ boundary allowed, is $C^2$ diffeomorphic to a compact smooth surface with smooth boundary. For a compact cooriented embedded surface in a smooth three-manifold, the diffeomorphism can be obtained by arbitrarily small local ambient displacements. This also applies to a compact intrinsic subsurface of a $C^2$ leaf: compactness is in the leaf topology, and its boundary is regular in that topology.

A connected oriented closed such surface with Euler characteristic zero is $C^2$ diffeomorphic to $T^2$. A compact regular surface region homeomorphic to a closed disk is $C^2$ diffeomorphic to $D^2$, and any prescribed $C^2$ diffeomorphism of its boundary circle can be realized by the disk parametrization.

Two disjoint regular closed disk regions in a $C^2$ sphere can simultaneously be carried to the standard two disk windows by a $C^2$ diffeomorphism, with compatible prescribed boundary parametrizations. A $C^2$ scalar function defined on a neighborhood of a compact set in $\mathbb R^2$ admits smooth approximations uniformly with its derivatives through order two on that compact set.

Finally let $L$ be a $C^2$ surface and $u:D^2\to L$ an **intrinsically continuous** map which is $C^2$ on an open boundary collar. On any smaller closed boundary collar contained in that open collar, $u$ has arbitrarily close $C^2$ approximations agreeing with $u$ on a neighborhood of the smaller collar, and a homotopy to each approximation fixed there. Closeness is uniform for any fixed compatible metric on $L$. No injectivity or immersion of the cap map is required.

Assume countable choice. For $n=2$ or $3$, a smoothly embedded closed $n$-ball in a connected boundaryless smooth $n$-manifold can be carried to a sufficiently small coordinate round ball by a smooth ambient isotopy. Consequently, a smooth closed disk in the boundary of a smooth $3$-ball is a standard disk window: the pair consisting of the ball and that disk is diffeomorphic to a round ball with a hemispherical boundary disk. Attaching a smooth $3$-ball to a smooth manifold along one such disk window does not change the diffeomorphism type, after smoothing the corner. The same conclusion holds in reverse, when a ball meeting the boundary in one disk is removed; the diffeomorphism is supported near the attached or removed ball and its attaching collar.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice-principle-for-foliation-pair]]). Let $S$ be an oriented Hausdorff $C^2$ surface without boundary, possibly disconnected. Then:

1. Every compact subset $K\subset S$ lies in the interior of a compact finitely cellulated $C^2$ subsurface $N$. If $K$ is contained in one connected component of $S$, $N$ can be chosen connected. A specified finite embedded regular $C^2$ graph contained in $\operatorname{Int}N$ can be included in its one-skeleton.
2. Every connected closed compact subsurface has an oriented genus normal form: the sphere for $g=0$, or the polygon word $\prod_{i=1}^g a_i b_i a_i^{-1}b_i^{-1}$ for $g\ge1$, with $\chi=2-2g$. A connected compact subsurface with $b>0$ boundary circles has a free fundamental group; capping its boundaries defines genus $g$ and gives $\chi=2-2g-b$ and free rank $2g+b-1$.
3. The fundamental group of every connected component of $S$ is torsion-free.
4. Every regular embedded $C^2$ nullhomotopic circle $c$ bounds an embedded compact disk region in $S$. Here a disk region is a compact subsurface homeomorphic to the closed disk, with boundary exactly $c$; its inherited surface structure and boundary are $C^2$. It is unique unless the **connected component containing $c$** is a sphere; in that component the two complementary disk regions are the two possibilities.

The normal forms in clause 2 are homeomorphism normal forms. No general differentiable smoothing theorem or arbitrary-surface triangulation-existence theorem is a premise of this item.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

derivations.claim: After smoothing corners, the prescribed boundary of an endomorphism surface has exactly $k$ circles: each arc at the bottom joins its identical top arc by its two vertical boundary intervals. A compact connected orientable surface with boundary embeds as one half of its smooth double: glue two copies along the reflected boundary collar. Thus the compact-subsurface formulas in [F6] apply to it. For genus $g$ and $b>0$ boundary circles they give $\chi=2-2g-b\le b$, with equality exactly when $g=0,b=1$, a topological disk. By [F4] it is a smooth disk with the prescribed boundary collar. For a closed connected orientable surface [F6] gives $\chi=2-2g$: the genus zero surface is a sphere, the genus one surface a torus, and all others have negative Euler characteristic. Their smooth disk or torus identifications are supplied by [F4]; the sphere follows by gluing its two smooth disk regions with the collar-compatible boundary parametrizations there. Summing over the boundary-bearing components gives $\chi\le k$, with equality only for $k$ disks.

We record why a disk system with these fixed boundary circles is unique relative to its boundary collars. More generally, two finite systems of disjoint smooth proper disks in a standard three-ball, with the same boundary curves, are isotopic relative to the boundary. For a nonempty system choose a boundary curve $\gamma$ bounding a boundary disk $Q$ whose interior contains no other boundary curve; For [F6], a stereographic chart avoiding a point outside each curve gives its required nullhomotopy by linear contraction in the plane; finite nesting then supplies the innermost curve. If $E$ is the proper disk with boundary $\gamma$, the union $E\cup Q$, rounded using the fixed collar, is a sphere: push the interior of $Q$ a little outside the ball before rounding, keeping its seam collar fixed. By [F2] the side of this sphere adjacent to the interior of $Q$ is a standard ball. It lies on that side of $E$ inside the original ball, apart from the small outside collar of $Q$: the complementary part of the original boundary sphere is connected and lies on the other side, as is checked first near the seam and then by disjointness. Removing the added collar therefore gives a ball region bounded by $E$ and $Q$. No other disk of the system lies inside it, since each has boundary outside $Q$ and is disjoint from $E$.

A degree zero generator has $\chi=k$. If it contains a sphere it vanishes by S. Otherwise its closed components have nonpositive Euler characteristic, so the inequality in step 1.1 forces every boundary-bearing component to be a disk and every closed component to be a torus. Delete all tori by T, giving $2^t$ times a disk system. For $k=0$, the remaining system is the empty surface. In particular a negative Euler characteristic closed component cannot survive by being balanced against any boundary-bearing component; its only possible positive compensation would have been a sphere, already zero.

To exclude torsion of that identity, define an integer evaluation of any closed orientable embedded surface by ignoring its embedding and assigning $0$ to a sphere, $2$ to a torus, and $0$ to any negative Euler characteristic component, then multiplying over components; the empty product is $1$. This evaluation respects S and T. It also respects four-tube relations. Indeed components not meeting the four patches give a common factor. If there is a negative Euler characteristic component all four evaluations vanish: a tube on one component lowers its Euler characteristic by two, while a tube merging two components replaces their Euler characteristics by their sum minus two. Even merging with a sphere therefore leaves negative Euler characteristic. If there are at least two spheres, every tube attachment leaves a sphere or merges two spheres to a sphere, so again every evaluation vanishes. With no spheres and only tori, attaching a tube creates a negative Euler characteristic component, and all four values vanish. The remaining case is exactly one sphere and $r$ tori. A tube meeting the sphere in zero, one or two patches has value respectively $0,2^r,2^{r+1}$: in the middle case it merges the sphere with one torus; in the last case it turns the sphere into a torus. Thus its value is $2^r$ times the number of its two patches on the sphere. Both sides of four-tube count each patch once, so their values agree.

Sweep $E$ through this ball region to a fixed disk parallel and very close to $Q$, keeping its boundary collar fixed. In ball coordinates this is the family of disk slices between the two hemispherical faces, stationary in a thin equatorial collar; rounding and a smooth reparametrization make the sweep smooth. Apply the ball-window assertion of [F5] to this actual ball region and its face $Q$, retaining the chosen seam collar; the complementary face is then the opposite hemispherical disk. This supplies the ball coordinates used in the sweep, rather than extending an arbitrary sphere diffeomorphism. The moving part is compactly contained away from the original boundary after deleting its stationary collar. Extend its velocity by the construction of [F3], cut it off before that boundary collar and before the other disks, and use its ambient flow. The velocity is zero where the sweep is stationary, so this extension fixes the entire original boundary and all other disks. Do this for either of the two systems, using the same final parallel disk. Cut off its small boundary ball. The remaining region is again a standard ball by the boundary-ball removal assertion of [F5]. Repeat for the remaining boundary curves. Finite induction identifies both systems with the same successive boundary-parallel disks, and hence with each other. Applying this to the vertical curtain disks proves that the system in step 2.1 is isotopic to $P\times[0,1]$. Thus every degree zero endomorphism is an integral multiple of the identity.

Outside the cylinder cap each of the $k$ prescribed boundary circles by a fixed disjoint once-punctured torus. Such caps exist: take the complementary boundary-parallel disks to the standard curtain system in a second ball and attach to each a tiny handle in its own disjoint neighbourhood. Gluing and applying step 2.2 gives a linear functional on the quotient endomorphism group, since any relation in the cylinder remains the same local relation after closure. On the curtain identity it has value $2^k$, including value $1$ for $k=0$. Hence $n\operatorname{id}_P=0$ implies $n2^k=0$ in $\mathbb Z$, and therefore $n=0$. Combined with step 3.1 this proves the asserted ring isomorphism.

A one-term complex has no nonzero homotopies between endomorphisms because the target in cochain degree $-1$ is zero. Its degree zero endomorphism ring is therefore the ring just computed. Its invertible elements are precisely the integers $+1,-1$, since $nm=1$ in $\mathbb Z$ forces that pair of possibilities. A common grading shift leaves these degrees unchanged. This proves simplicity.

boundaries.evidence: Step 2.1 includes k=0; step 4.1 evaluates its empty closure as 1.
Step 2.1 kills every spherical generator and excludes negative components after S.
Step 1.1 and step 3.1 identify the one-disk curtain.
Step 2.1 handles all possible closed components, and step 2.2 checks their local relations.
Steps 1.2 and 3.1 keep the prescribed boundary collars fixed.
Statement assumes countable choice through the explicitly named smooth suppliers.
Step 4.1 proves injectivity of the scalar map by the nonzero integer 2^k.
Step 3.1 proves surjectivity of the scalar map by disk-system isotopy.

derivations.claim: Vertical gluing subtracts the Euler characteristic of the common smoothing, which is $|B|/2$, so $\chi(C'\circ C)-|B|/2=(\chi(C')-|B|/2)+(\chi(C)-|B|/2)$. For a planar template with input boundary sizes $b_i$ and output size $b_0$, its curtain has Euler characteristic $(b_0+\sum_i b_i)/2$, and gluing the inserted surfaces subtracts $\sum_i b_i$ from Euler characteristic. Thus the output degree is $\sum_i(\chi(C_i)-b_i/2)$. Circle curtains contribute zero throughout. S, T and four-tube are homogeneous (a tube lowers Euler characteristic by two); planar insertion and stacking take each local relation to the same local relation in a larger surface. They therefore descend to degree-additive multilinear operations on the quotient and its shifts and finite sums.

Let $u:C\to C'$ and $v:C'\to C$ have $vu\simeq1_C$ and $uv\simeq1_{C'}$. Conjugation $[f]\mapsto[vfu]$ identifies the degree zero endomorphism rings of $C'$ and $C$: the inverse is $[g]\mapsto[ugv]$, and each composite reduces to the identity using the two inverse equations. These ring maps preserve identity and integral scalars, hence carry units to units and $\pm1$ to $\pm1$. Therefore simplicity of either complex implies simplicity of the other.

On a summand of multidegree $(r_i)$ in the total complex, applying the $i$th differential twice gives zero. For $i<j$, the coefficient for first applying $d_i$ and then $d_j$ is the negative of that for applying them in the reverse order, because only the first route increments the exponent preceding $d_j$. The two underlying surfaces agree by interchange of disjoint insertions. Hence the total differential squares to zero. Boundedness and finite direct sums ensure that each displayed total term is a finite sum. Shifts add, so every differential still has internal degree zero. Associativity of insertion and of the total degree sum identifies nested totalizations, and the sign exponent is the sum over earlier factors in either grouping.

For a homogeneous cochain map $f$ of degree $a$ in slot $i$, its insertion is multiplied by $(-1)^{a\sum_{j<i}r_j}$. In particular chain maps of cochain degree zero insert with no sign. If $h$ is a homotopy in that slot, insert it with sign $(-1)^{\sum_{j<i}r_j}$, since its degree is $-1$. In $dH+Hd$, the terms differentiating slot $i$ combine to insert $dh+hd$, with the two prefix signs cancelling. A term differentiating an earlier slot acquires one extra minus from the change in prefix degree; a term differentiating a later slot acquires one extra minus from the decrease in slot $i$ degree. Thus all other-slot terms cancel. Consequently insertion sends $f-g=dh+hd$ to the corresponding homotopy relation. Replacing several inputs successively proves the assertion for all inputs. Applied to both inverse equations, it shows that inserted homotopy equivalences remain homotopy equivalences.

For adjoining inverse boundary crossings, insert each assumed local inverse equivalence into the surrounding complex. Step 3.1 supplies natural isomorphisms $BA\cong\operatorname{Id}$ and $AB\cong\operatorname{Id}$ on the homotopy categories: naturality is the interchange identity between a map in the surrounding slot and the local degree zero map in the crossing slot. The two adjacent legs are precisely what makes these local replacements straight identity templates. No relation for any other Reidemeister move enters.

For completeness these functors identify endomorphism rings. If $\eta_C:C\to BA(C)$ is the natural isomorphism, applying $B$ followed by conjugation by $\eta_C$ is a left inverse to the endomorphism map induced by $A$, by naturality. Thus $A$ is faithful. The isomorphism $AB\cong\operatorname{Id}$ gives faithfulness of $B$ in the same way. If $f:A(C)\to A(C)$, set $g=\eta_C^{-1}B(f)\eta_C$. Naturality of $\eta$ gives $B(A(g))=\eta_C g\eta_C^{-1}=B(f)$; faithfulness of $B$ implies $A(g)=f$. Hence the endomorphism map is also surjective. It is a unital ring isomorphism preserving all integral scalars. Units are therefore $\pm1$ on one side exactly when they are so on the other, proving the final assertion.
